From Specific to Generic

Section 01 — One Repository to Rule Them All

The Copy-Paste Pain

In Session 02 we built PlanRepository. It works. But our gym has 9 entities. Are we really going to write nine repositories with the same five methods each?

public class PlanRepository
{
    private readonly GymDbContext _context;
    public PlanRepository(GymDbContext ctx) => _context = ctx;

    public IEnumerable<Plan> GetAll() => _context.Plans.ToList();
    public Plan? GetById(int id) => _context.Plans.Find(id);
    public void Add(Plan p) => _context.Plans.Add(p);
    public void Update(Plan p) => _context.Plans.Update(p);
    public void Delete(Plan p) => _context.Plans.Remove(p);
}

If we keep going…

File Lines What's different?
PlanRepository.cs ~25 —
MemberRepository.cs ~25 Replace Plan → Member
TrainerRepository.cs ~25 Replace Plan → Trainer
SessionRepository.cs ~25 Replace Plan → Session
… × 9 entities ~225 Just the type name

The smell: 200+ lines of code where the only thing that changes between files is a type name. That's not abstraction — that's duplication waiting to bite us. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) says we're doing something wrong.

👆 Click to reveal

What is a Generic Repository?

A Generic Repository is one class — parameterized by entity type T — that provides the standard CRUD operations for any entity in your database. Write it once, use it everywhere.

Wins

  • One implementation = one place to fix bugs
  • ~25 lines instead of ~225
  • Easy to add new entities

Trade-offs

  • Hides entity-specific query needs
  • Doesn't handle Include / projections
  • Pair with specific repos when needed

👆 Click to reveal

When NOT to Use the Generic Repo

Generic repos shine for vanilla CRUD. They struggle the moment your query is interesting — eager loading, filtering, projections. Know when to reach past them.

Scenario Generic repo?
"Get me a Member by Id" ✅ Yes — exactly what it's for
"Get me a Member with their HealthRecord and Bookings loaded" ❌ No — needs Include; use a specific repo
"Find all members whose membership expires this week" ❌ No — entity-specific query

The escape hatch — entity-specific repo extends the generic

public class MemberRepository : GenericRepository<Member>, IMemberRepository
{
    public MemberRepository(GymDbContext ctx) : base(ctx) { }

    // Inherits GetAll/GetById/Add/Update/Delete from the base ✓
    // Add ONLY the Member-specific queries here:
    public Member? GetWithHealthRecord(int id) =>
        _dbSet.Include(m => m.HealthRecord)
              .FirstOrDefault(m => m.Id == id);
}

Building the Member Module

Section 02 — Service · Controller · Views · Data Containers

MemberController — The 7 Actions

A standard CRUD controller has 5 user operations mapped to 7 action methods — because Create, Edit, and Delete each need a GET (show form / confirm) and a POST (commit changes).

Action HTTP URL Purpose
Index GET /Member List all members
Details GET /Member/Details/5 Show one member's details
Create GET /Member/Create Show empty form
Create POST /Member/Create Save submitted form
Edit GET /Member/Edit/5 Show form pre-filled
Edit POST /Member/Edit/5 Save edits
Delete POST /Member/Delete/5 Delete after confirmation

Why a Service Layer?

Repositories know how to fetch and save. Controllers know about HTTP and views. Neither should know about the rules of your business. Enter the service layer — the home for application logic.

The smell to avoid: Putting business rules in the controller — "if member's age < 16, return error" — makes the rule untestable, untransferable, and impossible to reuse from an API controller

👆 Click to reveal

ViewModels — What & Why?

A ViewModel is a plain C# class shaped for a specific view. It carries only the fields that view needs — nothing more, nothing less. Think of it as the entity, trimmed and reshaped for one screen.

🗄️
Entity
All DB fields + navigation properties
→
🎯
ViewModel
Only fields the view actually needs
→
🖥️
View
Renders HTML from the ViewModel

What happens if we skip the ViewModel?

Risk What goes wrong
Overposting attack Attacker submits hidden fields like IsAdmin=true → model binder writes them straight to the entity
Lazy-loading explosion View accidentally accesses navigation properties → triggers extra DB queries (N+1)
Tight coupling Rename a DB column → every view using the entity breaks
Validation pollution UI rules (Required, EmailAddress…) get mixed with DB constraints on the same class

Rule of thumb: One ViewModel per view shape. Index and Details can share one. Create and Edit usually need their own (Edit needs Id, Create doesn't).

Client-Side Validation — Catch Errors Before They Hit the Server

Client-side validation runs in the user's browser before the form is submitted. The user gets instant feedback — and your server is spared a round-trip just to say "this email is invalid".

🔄 The flow — with vs without client validation

❌ Without client validation
  1. User submits form
  2. HTTP request → server
  3. Server validates → finds errors
  4. Server returns the form with errors
  5. Page reloads, user sees errors

Slow. Wasteful. Bad UX.

✅ With client validation
  1. User types in a field
  2. Browser checks rule instantly
  3. If invalid → inline error appears
  4. Submit button blocked until all fields valid
  5. Only valid data reaches the server

Fast. Cheap. Great UX.

🧩 Three ingredients to enable it

1️⃣ Data Annotations

On the ViewModel: [Required], [EmailAddress], [StringLength], [RegularExpression]…

2️⃣ Tag Helpers in the View

asp-for on inputs, asp-validation-for for the error span, asp-validation-summary for the list.

3️⃣ Validation Scripts

Reference _ValidationScriptsPartial (jQuery Validate + Unobtrusive) at the bottom of the view.

🔬 How it works behind the scenes

Tag Helpers read your data annotations and emit data-val-* attributes on the rendered HTML. The unobtrusive jQuery library reads those attributes and wires up the validation rules — no JavaScript you have to write.

⚠️ Never trust the client. Client-side validation is a UX optimisation, not a security boundary. Always re-validate on the server with ModelState.IsValid — a user can disable JavaScript or POST directly with a tool.

👆 Click to reveal

ViewBag · ViewData · TempData — At a Glance

The @model directive is for the main data of a view. But sometimes you need a side channel — a dropdown list, a flash message, a page title. ASP.NET Core gives you three. They look similar; their lifetimes are very different.

Container Type Scope / Lifetime Storage
ViewBag dynamic Current request only Wrapper around ViewData
ViewData IDictionary<string, object> Current request only In-memory dictionary
TempData IDictionary<string, object> Survives one redirect Session or cookie (configurable)

The Update Member Page — What Can We Edit?

The Edit page is a focused form. Not every field of the member is editable here — some are shown for context only, others can be changed.

🗂️ Fields split by purpose

👁️ Display Only (read-only)
  • 📷 Photo
  • 👤 Name

Shown for context — not part of the form post-back.

✏️ Editable
  • 📧 Email
  • 📱 Phone
  • 🏠 Address → BuildingNumber · Street · City

These fields are bound to the ViewModel and validated.

📜 Business Rules to Enforce on Update

  • Email must remain unique — no other member can have the same email
  • Phone must remain unique — no other member can have the same phone
  • Egyptian phone format still applies: (010|011|012|015)XXXXXXXX
  • Email format must be valid

Why fewer fields than Create? Some data is locked after registration (Name, Gender, Date of Birth)

👆 Click to reveal

The Delete Confirmation Page — Are You Sure?

Delete is the most destructive action — it needs an extra step. The GET request shows a confirmation page; the POST request actually deletes. This protects users from accidental deletes triggered by misclicks or link crawlers.

📋 What does Delete need?

🔑 Member Id
Passed in the URL (e.g. /Member/Delete/5) — identifies which member to delete
⚠️ User Confirmation
Clicking Yes POSTs to the server — this is the actual delete

📜 Business Rules to Enforce on Delete

  • Cannot delete members with active bookings — block the delete if the member has any active reservation/session
  • Action is permanent — no soft-delete, no undo (as the warning banner says)

Plan — Index Page

The Plan listing uses a card-based layout — one card per plan package. Each card shows a summary plus action buttons. Plan data is seeded at application startup (no public Create action).

📋 Fields shown on each card

🔑 Id
int — hidden, used in action URLs
🏷️ Name
e.g. "Basic Plan"
💰 Price
decimal (EGP)
📅 Duration
int (days, e.g. 30, 60, 90, 365)
📝 Description
string
🟢 IsActive
bool — drives header colour & button label

🎬 Actions on each card

👁️ View Details
opens /Plan/Details/{id}
✏️ Edit
opens /Plan/Edit/{id}
🔄 Activate / Deactivate
toggles IsActive — replaces hard delete

📜 Business Rules

  • Seeded Data: Plans are inserted at startup — there is no public Create action
  • Active plans render with a blue header and a "Deactivate" button
  • Inactive plans render with a gray header and an "Activate" button
  • No hard delete — toggle IsActive instead (members may still reference inactive plans historically)

Plan — Edit Page

The Edit page lets administrators tweak plan pricing, duration, and description — but the plan name is locked to keep historical references stable.

🗂️ Fields split by purpose

👁️ Display Only (locked)
  • 🏷️ Plan Name — cannot be updated

Shown for context. The server rejects any change to it.

✏️ Editable (all required)
  • 📅 Duration (days)
  • 💰 Price (EGP)
  • 📝 Description

All three are required — note the red asterisks in the form.

📜 Business Rules to Enforce on Plan Edit

  • Plan Name cannot be updated — even if the form is tampered with, the service must reject any change to the name
  • Cannot update or deactivate a plan with active memberships — preserve the contract members signed up for

👆 Click to reveal

Plan — Activate / Deactivate Toggle

Plans are never hard-deleted. Instead, clicking Activate or Deactivate flips the IsActive flag, then redirects back to the Index — with a flash message confirming the change.

📜 Business Rules

  • No hard delete — the toggle is the only way to retire a plan
  • Cannot deactivate a plan with active memberships — protect existing contracts
  • The toggle is reversible — Inactive can be re-Activated at any time
  • Flash message "Plan Status Changed" confirms the action and disappears on next navigation
